title: Feature flags: release control without permanent branching
outcome: Use a flag to limit exposure and define defaults, ownership, removal, and data compatibility.
useCase: Controlled rollout of a risky workflow change.
benefits: Smaller exposure and deliberate rollback decisions.
drawbacks: State combinations, provider failure, and stale flags add complexity.
version: Pinned local examples · version-labelled configuration fragments
cue: Deploy code. Control exposure. Retire the switch.

trace.title: Owned flag
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

A feature flag changes which behavior is active for a context. It can separate deployment from exposure and help a controlled rollout.

It does not undo data already written or remove the need to test both paths.

Define the flag owner, intended lifetime, targeting inputs, safe default, and removal plan. Evaluate permissions on the server regardless of a client flag.

A client-visible flag is not a secret access gate.

A flag provider is another dependency. Decide whether evaluation is local/cached/remote and what happens when it is unavailable.

Keep the old/new schema compatible during overlap. Avoid combining many flags into untested state combinations.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Request context → flag decision → chosen behavior → observable outcome → guarded expansion → retire old path. Log a bounded variant tag where useful so errors can be compared.

Rehearse disabling the flag after the new path has written data. If the old path cannot read that data, the flag is not an effective rollback.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
A flag can become permanent dead code. A frontend flag does not authorize a server action.

Untested combinations can multiply behavior states.
